text: Your favorite YouTube hosts, you know who I’m talking about, promotes this app and swears up and down that they depend on it for information. So many hosts shill this so often I broke down, paid for a year and tried Ground News. I wasted my money buying this and as of today will stop wasting my time reading it. What you actually get here is an aggregator of news articles, most of which are foreign sites you’ve never heard of and contain no original reporting. You will find the same, exact news service (Associated Press, Reuters, etc.) article reprinted word for word in a large percentage of the sites presented for your consumption. The app’s characterization of each news source, right, left or center, high, low or medium factuality, appears to be a random creation of some chatbot. Ground News will give varying ratings of factual accuracy to the same wire service article when published on different sites. I can go on about each of the features of the site, but I’ll keep it simple; it’s a bunch of AI generated slop. So, if you like to read wire service articles printed on obscure foreign sites so you can tell your friends “ I read this article in The Vienna Express” in order to show off, this is your app. If that’s not your game, save your money and look elsewhere for your news sources.

Additionally, I have noticed on several occasions that the app headlines can be more critical of the topic and not align with any of the supporting headlines for articles listed. title: Gives false perception of being unbiased.
text: Because ground news only relies on two rating sources for bias determination, they do a poor job on their bias ratings. There is a high tendency to list left leaning sources as having mixed or low factuality. When challenged by this observation, GN absolves themselves by simply saying ‘hey, we just report what ad fontes and media bias fact check tell us. I have pointed out several times that the left leaning sources such as cnn, NYT, WAPO NPR, and others will often place subtle statements of opinion in their titles or choose what to report while conveniently leaving out important facts that would change the truth of story if it were presented. Example - AP is listed as highly factual yet it has pieces like the one about Israeli department of justice indicting Jewish settlers for violence … a true statement… but then adds in the title that the indictment is a rare occurrence. This is not simply a matter of bias. It is an opinion to rate whether something occurs rarely without providing more facts to justify that statement. What do they mean by rare? What is the definition of? 1 in a 100 cases, 1 in a 1000 or one in 10. Moreover what one person considers rare is often based on opinion. So the title may sem factually correct, but it loses its factual relevance once the title adds an editorial element. This is not merely bias, rather it is factually debatable. These same sources refused to cover stories like Hunter Biden Laptop when it first came out. Or the many leaks about Biden’s mental and cognitive decline. By not covering these and other stories they not only demonstrated bias, but also an inability to be truthful and transparent …Aka… dedicated to telling the facts about important events. Calling a news agency that hides critical facts or buries them deep in the article is anything but a highly factual organization. To say otherwise is simple argument through semantics. I cancelled my subscription after 2 years of asking them to reform with no luck.

title: The "Blindspot" feature has its own blindspot
text: As an independent political moderate, I downloaded Ground News specifically to escape tribal echo chambers. While it's a great concept, the app's factuality labels suffer from a massive systemic slant. Because the platform aggregates scores from just three specific watchdog organizations, it inherits their academic and institutional blind spots. Legacy outlets that aggressively push left-leaning narratives get labeled "High Factuality" simply because they use standard corporate journalistic mechanics, while the right-leaning ecosystem is penalized across the board. If the watchdogs keeping score lean left, an aggregator that relies solely on them will inevitably reflect that slant. It’s still a useful app to see what different sides are covering, but as a centrist looking for objective reality, I can't trust the factuality meters blindly. They tell you more about the biases of the fact-checkers than the actual truth of the reporting.

title: Not very helpful …
text: At one time, there was an app, of which I unfortunately no longer recall the name, that was extremely helpful concerning voting. Not only could one gain helpful, unbiased information concerning the candidates, as well as informationfrom the candidates themselves, but one could also get a sample ballot for a specific district, and mark those candidates for whom one wanted to vote. This was extremely helpful in expediting the process of filling in a sometimes lengthy ballot at a crowded polling place. Also, it was amazingly accessible for those of us who, out of necessity, use screen readers. Sadly, that app went the way of the dinosaur a couple of years ago, so I began seeking a replacement, hoping We Vote would fill the bill. Sadly, it did not. First: if you are not big into social media, are not affiliated with a specific political party, or are not involved in quasi-political organizations that support very specific issues, you get no information about candidates here. If a candidate isn’t registered specifically with We Vote, and if We Vote doesn’t have a link to the candidate’s website (if there is one), you get nowhere. As for marking candidates on a ballot: though, in theory, a sample ballot comes up, if you choose a specific candidate, it doesn’t mark the candidate’s name on the ballot, but assumes that you are supporting him/her in other ways. I am not big into social media, and neither are many of my friends; so, there is no help there. I am not involved with organizations who tend to endorse candidates; so, no help there, either. Finally, We Vote is not easy to navigate when using a screen reader. I’m sure it’s helpful for those who fit into all of the previously-mentioned categories—and who do not use screen readers—but for some of us, it is really a disappointment. And, by the way, the app refused to accept my address at first, so I’m not sure how accurate the information is that I was given, supposedly for my specific district.
